claim: prediction_detector.ts (γ3) is designed to fire on every assistant answer in the live consult chat, emit prediction_candidate stream parts, and calibration_producer.ts's recordCalibrationStamp writes one row to mcp_predictions per completion ('every chat completion through the adapter pipeline writes one row to mcp_predictions... independent of the LEL serve-time toggle').
reality: The detector is wired into the live request path, not dead code: platform/src/app/api/chat/consult/route.ts imports detectPredictionCandidates, and the shared onFinish write-through helper (onfinish_writethrough.ts) calls detectPredictionCandidates(...) unconditionally on opts.assistantText and separately calls recordCalibrationStamp(...) unconditionally after every completion, wrapped in try/catch (comment: 'Failures are swallowed — calibration logging must never break the user's response'). However mcp_predictions has 0 rows in the live DB despite chart_facts holding 276,206 rows (i.e. this is the populated production/build DB, not an empty dev DB), and conversations/conversation_messages both show 0 rows — meaning either the consult chat UI has never actually been exercised against this DB instance, or recordCalibrationStamp's writes are silently failing (the try/catch would hide that). No denominator of real chat turns is available in this DB to compute a fill rate; the honest statement is 0 observed writes against 0 observed chat turns, so runtime firing cannot be confirmed or denied from DB state alone.

evidence.quote: void recordCalibrationStamp({ chart_id: opts.chartId, ayanamsha_id: 'jh_true_chitra', query_text: opts.lastUserQuery, model_id: opts.modelId })
SELECT count(*) FROM mcp_predictions -> 0; SELECT count(*) FROM conversation_messages -> 0; SELECT count(*) FROM chart_facts -> 276206

recommended_action: Check application logs (out of DB-audit scope) for '[calibration_producer] recordCalibrationStamp DB error' to rule out silent write failure; if the consult route genuinely has zero production traffic, note that separately since it changes the risk profile of every other consult-path finding in this wave.

claim: (Implicit in the architecture doc's single pipeline diagram at §7) there is one coherent prediction ledger flowing answer→detection→ledger→outcome→calibration.
reality: There are two disjoint, unreconciled prediction-logging systems writing to two different tables with no FK or join key between them: (1) mcp_predictions — written by the chat-side prediction_detector/calibration_producer path on every consult completion (0 rows observed); id format PPL.CAL.xxxxxxxx. (2) mimamsa_predictions — written by the L5 orchestrator build writer mi_bhavisya per chart at build time (384 rows), transitioned to confirmed/denied by mi_abhilekha.py, and it is this table (not mcp_predictions) that mimamsa_calibration's prediction_id column and phala_anchors reference. The architecture doc's §7 diagram presents a single ledger; the codebase has built two independent prediction-tracking subsystems (a build-time/orchestrator one that is populated, and a chat-time/user-facing one that is empty) that do not share an id space.

recommended_action: Decide which of the two prediction subsystems is canonical for the 'ledger' the NO-LEAKAGE role design (§7.4) is meant to protect, and either retire/merge the other or document the split explicitly — as written, a reader of §7.4 cannot tell which physical table role_ledger_write is supposed to gate.

claim: PARIPRASHNA_TARGET_ARCHITECTURE_v0_1.md §7.4 'DB role grants — the NO-LEAKAGE enforcement' designs five DB roles (role_web_serve, role_orchestrator, role_ledger_write, role_jobs, role_sidecar) with role_web_serve explicitly denied ledger INSERT/UPDATE and mimamsa_calibration write, and role_ledger_write held ONLY by an out-of-process ledger writer.
reality: NONE of the five designed roles exist in the live database. `SELECT rolname FROM pg_roles` returns only Cloud SQL system/admin roles (cloudsqladmin, cloudsqlsuperuser, postgres, etc.) plus exactly one application role: amjis_app. amjis_app holds full CRUD (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER) on BOTH the populated real ledger (mimamsa_predictions, 384 rows with outcome data) and mimamsa_calibration — the two tables §7.4 explicitly designs role_web_serve to be blocked from writing. platform/src/lib/db/client.ts confirms the web app's own Next.js API routes (including the consult chat route and calibration_producer.ts) connect through a single Pool using one DB_USER credential — there is no second connection/credential used anywhere for an out-of-process 'ledger writer' role. A repo-wide grep for the five role names (role_web_serve, role_orchestrator, role_ledger_write, role_jobs, role_sidecar) across platform/, platform-mcp/, and infra/ returns zero matches — the design was never implemented, not even partially or in a migration that hasn't run.

evidence.quote: SELECT rolname FROM pg_roles ORDER BY rolname -> amjis_app, cloudsqladmin, cloudsqlagent, cloudsqlconnpooladmin, ... postgres (28 rows; only amjis_app is an application role; no role_web_serve/role_orchestrator/role_ledger_write/role_jobs/role_sidecar present)
grantee=amjis_app, table_name=mimamsa_predictions, privilege_type IN (SELECT,INSERT,UPDATE,DELETE,TRUNCATE,REFERENCES,TRIGGER); same full set on mimamsa_calibration and mcp_predictions
user: process.env.DB_USER!, password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD!, database: process.env.DB_NAME! — single Pool, single credential, used by every route including the web-serving consult chat path

§7.4 designs role_web_serve: 'SELECT layer tables, conv store R/W, pins R/W, ledger SELECT-status-only. NO ledger INSERT/UPDATE. NO mimamsa_calibration write.' and role_ledger_write: 'ledger + outcome + calibration write. Held ONLY by the out-of-process ledger writer.' — repo-wide grep for these five role name strings across platform/, platform-mcp/, infra/ returns zero matches

recommended_action: Treat §7.4's NO-LEAKAGE role separation as entirely unbuilt (0%), not partially built. Before any production reliance on 'the serving role cannot leak outcome data into new predictions,' either (a) create the five roles and re-grant per §7.4's boundary table, migrating the web app off amjis_app for read paths, or (b) explicitly downgrade the doc's claim from an enforced invariant to an application-level convention with no DB-level backstop, since today amjis_app — the same credential the web app uses to serve every request — has unrestricted write access to the prediction ledger and the calibration table it is supposed to be walled off from.
